title: Which Part of DNA Is the Code?

scenes.tts: A strawberry and a person use the same kind of D N A. What inside that molecule can help make them different? Both lead into cells, then toward the same twisting ladder. The puzzle is where differences sit.
scenes.caption: A strawberry and a person use the same kind of DNA. What inside that molecule can help make them different? Both lead into cells, then toward the same twisting ladder. The puzzle is where differences sit.
scenes.visual: Dark frame. A large cartoon strawberry fills the left and a same-height student silhouette fills the right. Each smoothly zooms into a labelled cell, then both cells slide around one shared block-ladder labelled 'DNA (schematic)'. Keep the world on screen. COLOR MAP for both films: sugar-phosphate sides BLUE; A/T base blocks YELLOW; C/G base blocks GREEN; gene TEAL; protein RED; trait GOLD; counts and axes GREY/WHITE. No molecular structure.
scenes.narration: A strawberry and a person use the same kind of DNA. What inside that molecule can help make them different? Both lead into cells, then toward the same twisting ladder. The puzzle is where differences sit.

scenes.visual: Keep the large shared ladder faintly turning in place. Add the title 'Which Part of DNA Is the Code?' for two seconds, then transform the title into a small question mark beside the ladder.

scenes.tts: D N A is a double helix, like a ladder twisted along its length. Sugar and phosphate form both sides. Those side parts are the same kinds in every living thing. The useful difference is not the frame around the rungs.
scenes.caption: DNA is a double helix, like a ladder twisted along its length. Sugar and phosphate form both sides. Those side parts are the same kinds in every living thing. The useful difference is not the frame around the rungs.
scenes.visual: The carried block-ladder fills most of the frame. It slowly untwists to a flat ladder, then twists again. Blue rails pulse when 'sugar and phosphate' is said. Small strawberry, mushroom, bacterium and person icons glide past the same blue rails. Label the drawing 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: DNA is a double helix, like a ladder twisted along its length. Sugar and phosphate form both sides. Those side parts are the same kinds in every living thing. The useful difference is not the frame around the rungs.

scenes.tts: The rungs carry base pairs. Each base has a letter name: A, T, C, or G. In ordinary double-stranded D N A, A pairs with T. C pairs with G. Pairing lets either side tell us the partner across each rung.
scenes.caption: The rungs carry base pairs. Each base has a letter name: A, T, C, or G. In ordinary double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T. C pairs with G. Pairing lets either side tell us the partner across each rung.
scenes.visual: Flatten the same ladder. Build each rung from two large labelled blocks. A and T use yellow outlines; C and G use green outlines. One side rises slightly while its partners stay aligned across from it. A small 'base pair' bracket grows around one whole rung.
scenes.narration: The rungs carry base pairs. Each base has a letter name: A, T, C, or G. In ordinary double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T. C pairs with G. Pairing lets either side tell us the partner across each rung.

scenes.tts: Two ladders have matching blue sides. Their rung letters appear in different orders. Which part can carry different instructions: the shared sides or the changing base order? Hold your answer while a small reader waits at the first rung.
scenes.caption: Two ladders have matching blue sides. Their rung letters appear in different orders. Which part can carry different instructions: the shared sides or the changing base order? Hold your answer while a small reader waits at the first rung.
scenes.visual: Split the carried ladder into two full-height ladders with identical blue rails. Reorder only the yellow and green base blocks. Put the spoken question across the top and a small white reader arrow at the first rung. Gentle base-block glow continues.
scenes.narration: Two ladders have matching blue sides. Their rung letters appear in different orders. Which part can carry different instructions: the shared sides or the changing base order? Hold your answer while a small reader waits at the first rung.

scenes.visual: Keep both ladders and the full question visible. The reader arrow bobs once beside the first rung; no answer highlight appears during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: The changing order carries information. Sequence means base order along D N A. Traits are features of living things. Here is the rule connecting both films. D N A sequence helps shape traits; D N A amount does not rank organism complexity. This film builds the sequence half.
scenes.caption: The changing order carries information. Sequence means base order along DNA. Traits are features of living things. Here is the rule connecting both films. DNA sequence helps shape traits; DNA amount does not rank organism complexity. This film builds the sequence half.
scenes.visual: Dim both blue rails without removing them. The base blocks brighten. The reader arrow travels rung by rung down each sequence and copies visited blocks into a strip labelled 'sequence'. Add 'trait = feature', show the full rule once, then return focus to its sequence half.
scenes.narration: The changing order carries information. Sequence means base order along DNA. Traits are features of living things. Here is the rule connecting both films. DNA sequence helps shape traits; DNA amount does not rank organism complexity. This film builds the sequence half.

scenes.tts: A highlighted sequence sits within a gene, a section of D N A. A chromosome is packaged D N A and carries many genes. Many genes carry instructions used to build proteins. Other genes carry code used in other ways.
scenes.caption: A highlighted sequence sits within a gene, a section of DNA. A chromosome is packaged DNA and carries many genes. Many genes carry instructions used to build proteins. Other genes carry code used in other ways.
scenes.visual: The sequence strip shrinks into a teal bracket labelled 'gene' on a long blue DNA ribbon. The ribbon packages into one thick cartoon chromosome labelled 'schematic'. Several teal gene brackets slide into positions along it. One gene sends blocks toward a red block labelled 'protein'; another ends at a neutral 'other cell use' box.
scenes.narration: A highlighted sequence sits within a gene, a section of DNA. A chromosome is packaged DNA and carries many genes. Many genes carry instructions used to build proteins. Other genes carry code used in other ways.

scenes.tts: Follow one pea example. A working protein is needed to make purple flower colour. A change in its gene can stop that protein working. The flower can then be white. This case connects gene sequence, protein, and trait without making every trait simple.
scenes.caption: Follow one pea example. A working protein is needed to make purple flower colour. A change in its gene can stop that protein working. The flower can then be white. This case connects gene sequence, protein, and trait without making every trait simple.
scenes.visual: Carry one teal gene bracket to the left. Its base blocks feed a moving red block labelled 'protein', which turns a large pea-flower cartoon purple. Change one gene block; the red block stops before the flower, and a second flower opens white. Label the whole path 'one pea example' and 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Follow one pea example. A working protein is needed to make purple flower colour. A change in its gene can stop that protein working. The flower can then be white. This case connects gene sequence, protein, and trait without making every trait simple.

scenes.tts: The path is a first model, not a promise that each gene makes one trait. Many traits depend on several genes. Surroundings can matter too. Some base changes alter nothing you can see, so scientists test changes instead of guessing from letters alone.
scenes.caption: The path is a first model, not a promise that each gene makes one trait. Many traits depend on several genes. Surroundings can matter too. Some base changes alter nothing you can see, so scientists test changes instead of guessing from letters alone.
scenes.visual: The single pea path moves upward and gains labels 'first model' and 'schematic'. Below it, several teal gene strips and a simple sun/water surroundings icon converge with cautious arrows on one gold trait circle. A changed base appears on one strip while the trait circle remains a question mark.
scenes.narration: The path is a first model, not a promise that each gene makes one trait. Many traits depend on several genes. Surroundings can matter too. Some base changes alter nothing you can see, so scientists test changes instead of guessing from letters alone.

scenes.tts: Almost every skin and muscle cell in one person carries the same D N A. Yet each cell type uses different genes. Different proteins follow, so the cells look and work differently. The code matters together with how each cell uses it.
scenes.caption: Almost every skin and muscle cell in one person carries the same DNA. Yet each cell type uses different genes. Different proteins follow, so the cells look and work differently. The code matters together with how each cell uses it.
scenes.visual: A single long chromosome duplicates into matching copies inside a large skin-cell cartoon and muscle-cell cartoon. Different teal gene brackets glow in each cell. Distinct red blocks labelled 'proteins' build beneath them while the shared chromosomes remain matched. Keep a visible 'schematic' badge.
scenes.narration: Almost every skin and muscle cell in one person carries the same DNA. Yet each cell type uses different genes. Different proteins follow, so the cells look and work differently. The code matters together with how each cell uses it.

scenes.tts: Follow base order through a gene, protein, and trait. Shared parts can carry different sequences, and cells can use genes differently. So D N A sequence helps shape traits. Counting whole chromosome sets is a different question, for the second film.
scenes.caption: Follow base order through a gene, protein, and trait. Shared parts can carry different sequences, and cells can use genes differently. So DNA sequence helps shape traits. Counting whole chromosome sets is a different question, for the second film.
scenes.visual: Bring back the gene-to-protein-to-trait path on the left with a 'schematic' badge. On the right, transform a ladder into an unfilled bar-chart frame labelled 'DNA amount' and 'question—no data yet'. Show only the sequence half of the rule across the middle; the amount frame stays empty.
scenes.narration: Follow base order through a gene, protein, and trait. Shared parts can carry different sequences, and cells can use genes differently. So DNA sequence helps shape traits. Counting whole chromosome sets is a different question, for the second film.

scenes.visual: End card with one centered line only, large and high-contrast: 'DNA sequence helps shape traits.' No title, logo, URL, subtitle, or smaller line.
